solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Leading journalists drink squash

indicators.note: what leads comes first, so the drink is placed ahead of the journalists

explanation.surface: Senior reporters knocking back a fruit cordial.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Squash' looks like the drink, and 'drink' sits right beside it to help; but squash is the verb here, and the drink is only SUP.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to squash a revolt or a rumour is to crush it and keep it down.

clue.text: Sewer rats seem out of place aboard ship

indicators.note: letters that are out of place are not where they started, so RATS SEEM is rearranged

explanation.surface: Rats that look out of place on a vessel, heading for the drains.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sewer' is read as a drain for the rats; here it is someone who sews.
explanation.definitionFit: A pun on sewer: not a drain but one who sews, and a woman who sews for a living is the classic example.

clue.text: Audio streamed from school pitch

parts.note: a pod is a school of whales or dolphins
to pitch is to throw, or cast

explanation.surface: A recording broadcast from a school's playing field.
explanation.walkthrough: School and pitch suggest a sports field; one is a group of whales and the other a throw.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by description: a programme of recorded sound delivered over the internet, audio that is streamed or downloaded.

clue.text: Make, supply or apply plaster
Pompous type, loaded, ill-tempered mostly

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so SHIRTY loses its last letter

parts.note: SHIRTY (British slang: bad-tempered) without its Y

explanation.surface: A description of a pompous, wealthy, mostly bad-tempered man.
explanation.walkthrough: Shirty is British slang for irritable or cross.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: someone puffed up with self-importance, like a shirt stuffed to look full, is a pompous type.

clue.text: Gray's second compendium mostly contains elegies

indicators.note: the second of a word is its second letter
a thing that contains another holds it inside
mostly means not quite all, so DIGEST loses its final letter

explanation.surface: Thomas Gray's second anthology is largely elegiac.
explanation.walkthrough: Gray wrote the famous 'Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard', so the surface is apt; but 'Gray's second' is just his R.
explanation.definitionFit: Near synonyms: an elegy is a mournful poem and a dirge a mournful song, both laments for the dead.

clue.text: Nits spread by insects and ticks

indicators.note: spread means scattered about, so the letters of NITS are scattered into a new order

explanation.surface: Lice eggs carried about by insects and ticks.
explanation.walkthrough: Among nits and insects, 'ticks' looks like one more parasite; it is moments, as in 'back in a tick'.
explanation.definitionFit: Informal British usage: 'just a tick' means just a moment, so ticks are brief moments.

clue.text: Not all reading list entries are brilliant

indicators.note: not all of the words are used, only a run of letters from inside them

parts.note: the letters run from the end of 'reading', through 'list', into the start of 'entries'

explanation.surface: A reviewer's grumble that some books on the reading list are poor.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a plural verb phrase, matched by the plain verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A verb for a verb phrase: things that sparkle and shine in the light are being brilliant.

clue.text: Large number rubbed out

definitions.meaning: a great many, an informal word for a lot
gangster slang for killed; the old past tense of slay

explanation.surface: A big figure erased from the page.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rubbed out' suggests an eraser, but it is gangster slang for killed.
explanation.definitionFit: Two unrelated words that share a spelling: an informal word for a lot, and the past tense of slay.

clue.text: Rider and daughter finish in a ditch almost

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so DUMP loses its final letter

parts.note: A + DUMP (to ditch) without its P; D END goes after its D

explanation.surface: A horse rider and his daughter nearly ending up in a ditch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rider' pictures someone on horseback; a rider is also a clause added to a document.
explanation.definitionFit: A specialist sense: in law and politics a rider is a clause tacked on to a document, an addition at the end.

clue.text: Aim a bit higher than the church?

parts.note: the part of a church that rises above the rest

explanation.surface: Advice to set one's sights a little above the church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Aim a bit higher' reads as advice, but the wordplay is a cryptic hint for the part of a church that rises above the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to aim high and to set one's hopes on something are the same ambition.

clue.text: At sea each lounge is somewhere to relax

indicators.note: to be at sea is to be confused, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: On a cruise ship, every lounge is a place to unwind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Is' belongs to the fodder, not a link, which is easy to miss.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by description: a long reclining chair is literally a place to put one's feet up.

clue.text: Latest report by old newspaper character

explanation.surface: The latest dispatch from a figure at an old newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Newspaper character' suggests a cartoon figure or columnist, but the paper and the character are separate pieces, and character here means courage or spirit.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: the state of the art is the current peak of a technology, so anything described this way is the latest.

clue.text: Welfare checks statesmen forced on society

indicators.note: something forced is bent out of its natural shape, so the letters are wrenched into a new order

parts.note: S = society, added on to the fodder

explanation.surface: Politicians imposing benefit checks on the public.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram takes in STATESMEN and the S together.
explanation.definitionFit: A British term: benefits are granted only after checking a claimant's income and savings, their means.

clue.text: Hotel auditor's legal documents

indicators.note: an auditor is literally a hearer, so the answer is what a listener hears

explanation.surface: An accountant at a hotel with legal papers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Auditor' pictures an accountant; here it simply means a listener.
explanation.definitionFit: A proper name standing for the thing: the Ritz is a famous luxury hotel in London.

clue.text: Hand stopping a ball going in

indicators.note: a thing stopping a gap plugs it

explanation.surface: A goalkeeper's hand keeping out a ball heading into the net.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is football; 'ball' is a formal dance, not the thing being kicked.
explanation.definitionFit: A formal synonym: being allowed to enter a place is gaining entry, the act of going in.

clue.text: Golf club contracted with another in China

indicators.note: a contracted word is shortened, so WEDGE loses its last letter

parts.note: WEDGE, a golf club, without its E
a wood is another kind of golf club

explanation.surface: A golfer in China signing up with a club.
explanation.walkthrough: 'China' reads as the country, but it is porcelain.
explanation.definitionFit: A brand name for the thing: an English pottery firm famous for its fine china.

clue.text: Book about Hearts initially exaggerated their goal tally

parts.note: She, the novel by H. Rider Haggard

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so each of the last two words gives its first letter

explanation.surface: A book about Heart of Midlothian football club inflating its goal count.
explanation.walkthrough: Hearts is a Scottish football club, which is the picture; here it is just CORES. 'Their' looks like part of the definition but supplies its T.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by function: the sheet a scorer fills in during a match is where a team's goals are totted up.

clue.text: Cop turned killer in LA?

parts.note: milk that has turned has gone off
American slang: to ice someone is to kill them

explanation.surface: A Los Angeles policeman who became a murderer.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the slang: ICER is a killer only in US gangster talk, hence 'in LA'.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: cop is the informal word for a police officer.

clue.text: Italy's capital missing from simple map

indicators.note: a word's capital letter is its first, so Italy gives I
something missing from a word has been taken out of it

explanation.surface: Rome is missing from a basic map.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Italy's capital' wants to be Rome; it is only the letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: Near synonym: a street layout or floor layout drawn from above is a kind of map.

clue.text: Falling behind insulation

definitions.meaning: material wrapped round pipes and tanks to keep the heat in

explanation.surface: Falling behind with the insulation work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Behind insulation' reads as a location, but the clue splits after 'behind'.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: the verb form of trailing behind, and the plumbing noun for pipe wrapping.

clue.text: Note that's upset a Cheshire constituent

indicators.note: to upset something is to tip it over, and in a down entry that turns the word upside down

parts.note: a tenner is a ten-pound note

explanation.surface: A letter that has offended a voter in Cheshire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Constituent' pictures a voter in a Cheshire constituency; Cheshire is a cheese.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Cheshire is a British cheese, and this enzyme that curdles milk is one of its ingredients.

clue.text: Climber's knot — guess if he got tangled

indicators.note: tangled rope is twisted out of order, so the letters are twisted into a new one

explanation.surface: Wondering which knot a climber used, if he got his rope in a tangle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Guess' looks like anagram fodder beside 'tangled'; it is FIGURE, and only IF HE GOT is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A specialist term: climbers tie this knot, shaped like the numeral 8, to fasten the rope to a harness.

clue.text: Help to lower a pulse

indicators.note: to lower something is to move it down, and in a down entry the A moves down the word

parts.note: the letter A that moves down

explanation.surface: Aiding a heartbeat to slow down.
explanation.walkthrough: Only one letter moves: the A of ABET is taken down to third place.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: the pulse is the regular throb of the heart, each throb one unit of it.

clue.text: Key bank bond held by a third party

definitions.text: bond held by a third party

parts.note: the Escape key on a keyboard
a bank of seats or switches is a row

explanation.surface: A financial key: a bank bond looked after by someone else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bank' reads as the financial kind, but it is a row, as in a bank of lights.
explanation.definitionFit: A legal term: money or a deed lodged with a neutral party until a deal's conditions are met.

clue.text: Mature, since working for model employers

indicators.note: something working is in motion, so the letters are set moving into a new order

explanation.surface: Grown-up since taking a job with exemplary employers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Model employers' reads as ideal bosses; it means firms that hire out fashion models.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: firms that sign and book fashion models are the models' employers.

clue.text: Lecture dealing with India partitioning

indicators.note: to partition something is to divide it

parts.note: I = India in the phonetic alphabet, placed after T

explanation.surface: A talk on trade relations during the partition of India.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface recalls the 1947 Partition; here 'partitioning' just means I splits TRADE.
explanation.definitionFit: Near synonym: a long angry harangue is a telling-off lecture.

clue.text: Firstly, scout acquires inside info about reserves

indicators.note: about means turned around, so the assembled letters are read backwards
firstly means first of all, so scout gives only its first letter

explanation.surface: A talent scout gets inside information on the reserve players.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Inside info' looks like one phrase, but 'inside' is the container signal; the whole string is then turned round.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: money put aside for the future, a financial reserve.
